title: Haredi Judaism
hookLine: "those who tremble": close-knit communities devoted to Torah study

cards: Close to midnight, and the room is still full: tables, open books, and noise. Two people lean over one page of Talmud, and one is jabbing the margin with a finger.

Across the table, another pair argues the same line from the other side. Nobody shushes anybody. This is a study hall, a beit midrash, and in today's communities, a room like this sits near the center of life.
From outside, people tend to notice the dark coats and hats. From inside, people tend to talk about the page.

teach.h: YE THAT TREMBLE AT HIS WORD.
teach.b: Haredi. First, the name comes from a verse. Isaiah says: "Hear the word of the LORD, ye that tremble at his word."
In Hebrew, those who tremble is haredim. So the name isn't about fear of people. It describes awe before the word of God, a seriousness that shapes a whole life.
Second, study. God tells Joshua the book of the law should not leave his mouth: "thou shalt meditate therein day and night." Haredi communities take that line close to literally.

teach.h: DAY AND NIGHT: A LIFE OF STUDY.
teach.b: Boys and young men may spend long years in a yeshiva, and some married men keep learning in a kollel, a study hall for adults, while the family's life is arranged to support it.
Women learn too, in their own schools, and in some families carry much of the work outside the home. Third, community.
Haredi life is close-knit on purpose: its own schools, its own neighborhoods, a careful distance from much of the wider culture's media.
Inside, there are free-loan funds, meals brought to new mothers, and help for anyone in trouble. And it isn't one thing. Some communities are Hasidic, gathered around a rebbe.
Others center on the yeshivas and their heads. There are Sephardi Haredi communities too. Fourth, why study holds that place.
The Mishnah lists good deeds whose fruit a person enjoys in this world, honoring parents, acts of kindness, making peace between people, and ends: the study of Torah is equal to them all.
Elsewhere the sages ask which is greater, study or doing, and answer: study, because study leads to doing.
In this view, the open book is where every other good thing begins.

how: Haredi Jews keep halakha in full and build close-knit communities around Torah study, with yeshivas for young men, kollels for married men, schools for girls and women, and strong networks of mutual help.

games.q: the Mishnah lists honoring parents, acts of kindness, making peace between people, and one more. which does it call equal to them all?
games.why: the study of Torah is equal to them all, and the Talmud explains: study leads to doing.

practice: Bring to mind someone whose life is shaped by a devotion you don't share: a religious neighbor, an athlete in training, a grandparent who never missed a morning prayer.
Leave aside whether you'd live that way, and look at what it costs them, and what it gives them. If you pray, you can hold them in that prayer.

wordCard.voice: Haredi. Those who tremble at God's word, from Isaiah: close-knit communities, Hasidic and others, that put the study of Torah at the center of life. Today's word.
